An important point here seems to be two differing concepts of regret. On the one hand, regret leads to more agency in an individual. Other times the regret does not represent such expanded agency. It will be helpful to understand the two different senses of regret. Importantly, when a person lacks appropriate regret, they do so because of their inability to desire union with another which is caused by a lack of integration in themselves. Professor Stump here defends a Thomistic view which says that God could cooperate "with a person's own higher-order desires" and give them the power to will "some particular good" [@stum10, 160].

As such, Professor Stump defines sanctification as "a person is also loving God" in that in their God assisted desire to desire a good will, they are also desiring "internal integration" with God. In other words, a person can achieve integration within themselves when they ask for and accept God's help to ask for help to have appropriate desires. As such, the appropriate kind of regret is bestowed on individuals as an act of God's grace.
